title: Investment, Loan and Job Scams
intro: See how investment schemes, loan offers and job ads use the same pay-first trap, and learn the warning signs that give them away.
recap: Promises of fast, guaranteed returns are a warning sign. Early payouts come from later joiners' money.
A real employer pays you. A fee for training or a uniform before you start is a scam pattern.
A fee before a loan arrives is the trap. A real lender states every charge before you agree.
Screenshots of other people's payouts prove nothing about the next person.

aiTutor.recap: These scams use greed and hope. They offer money, a loan or a job, and ask for something first. The early payouts are real so that you will believe the rest.
aiTutor.example: Bisi sees friends posting that they were paid. She puts in 20,000 naira, and the first payout arrives. She then adds 100,000 naira from her savings. The second payout never comes, and the organiser's phone is off.
aiTutor.watchOut: Seeing people you know get paid feels like proof. It is not, because early payouts are the show that brings in later money.
aiTutor.tryThis: Next time you see an offer, ask: who pays whom, and when? If you pay first and the promise comes later, stop.

glossary.definition: Something attractive used to draw you in. In these scams, the early payouts and the promised returns are the bait.
glossary.example: Being paid 40,000 naira once is the bait. The hook is the much larger amount you are then asked to put in.

glossary.definition: A planned way of making money. A pyramid scheme pays earlier members with the money of newer members, so it lasts only while new people keep joining.
glossary.example: A scheme that cannot explain where its profit comes from, only that "people are joining", is a warning sign.

paragraphs: Made-up story: Bisi is told, "Put in 20,000 naira and in two weeks you get 40,000. Many people already did it. Here are their screenshots." The first few people really are paid. That is the bait. Real investments can lose money, so a promise of guaranteed returns with no risk is a warning sign.
Those early payments come from the money of the people who joined next. When not enough new people join, the scheme stops paying and the organiser disappears.

Loans and jobs have their own version. "You are approved for a loan, pay a processing fee first." "You are hired, pay for your uniform and training." The pattern is the same: pay first, receive nothing.

Be careful with loan apps too. Some ask to see your contacts and photos, then use them to shame or pressure borrowers. Before you install one, check what it asks permission to use, what its reviews say, and who runs it.

screens.title: How a "Double Your Money" Scheme Works

aiTutor.explain: Tap each step to see where the money really comes from. Follow one naira from the new member's pocket to the early member's payout. No profit is made along the way.
aiTutor.example: Ten people each pay 20,000 naira, so 200,000 naira goes in. If the organiser promises to double it, 400,000 naira is owed. The money is never there, so the last people lose everything.
aiTutor.watchOut: A scheme can look healthy for months. The collapse comes when new members stop joining, and nobody can say when that will be.

walkThrough.title: Following 100,000 naira through a "double your money" scheme
steps: Ten friends each pay in 10,000 naira. The organiser now holds 100,000 naira and promises to double it.
The first two friends are paid 20,000 naira each. That money comes from the other eight friends' payments, not from any profit.
The two paid friends tell everyone, and more people join. The scheme now looks real.
Newcomers slow down. There is not enough money to pay everyone what was promised.
The organiser's phone goes silent. The last people in lose what they paid.
What to do instead: before paying, ask where the profit really comes from. If the only answer is "more people joining", walk away.

nodes.label: 1. Joiners
nodes.title: People pay in
nodes.definition: Each new person pays money to join, hoping to double it. The organiser keeps all of it in one place.
nodes.bonusFact: The scheme needs a steady stream of new people to survive.

nodes.label: 2. Payouts
nodes.title: Early members are paid
nodes.definition: A few early members get paid, and they tell everyone. Their payment is made from the money of later joiners, not from any real profit.
nodes.bonusFact: Early payouts are a show. They make the scheme look real and bring in more people.

nodes.label: 3. Collapse
nodes.title: The money runs out
nodes.definition: New joiners slow down and there is not enough to pay everyone. The scheme stops, and the latest members lose what they paid.
nodes.bonusFact: The later you join, the more likely you are to lose, and the people you brought in lose too.

widgetData.completionMessage: You have followed the scheme from first payment to collapse.
widgetData.completionBonusFact: Real investments can lose money and never promise to double it quickly. A promise of no risk is a warning on its own, and so is pressure to bring in friends.

aiTutor.explain: Look for the part of the offer that cannot be true in real life. Platforms and minimum amounts vary, but nobody can guarantee a high return with no risk.
aiTutor.watchOut: A professional look, a registered-sounding name and a long list of testimonials are all easy to fake. They are not the red flag, and they are not proof either.

widgetData.question: An advert says: "Invest 50,000 naira and earn 30% every week, guaranteed, with zero risk." What is the biggest red flag?

options.text: A guaranteed, very high, weekly return with zero risk.
It is advertised on social media.

widgetData.explanation: Real investments carry risk, and nobody can guarantee high weekly returns. The promise is the trap, not the platform or the amount. If the offer sounds too good to need any risk, assume the risk is yours.
widgetData.bonusFact: The higher the promised return, the higher the chance that the promise is false. A fair rule: if you cannot explain how they make the money, do not give them yours.

screens.title: Loan or Job: Real or Scam?

aiTutor.explain: Decide whether each statement is true or false. Ask yourself who is paying whom, and when. The pattern in every scam here is that you pay first.
aiTutor.tryThis: For each card, say out loud what the scammer gets and what you get. If you get a promise and they get money, stop.

widgetData.instruction: Is each statement true or false?

cards.statement: A real employer asks you to pay a "training" or "uniform" fee before you start work.
cards.explanation: Employers pay you. Being asked to pay first is the advance fee pattern.
cards.bonusFact: Search the company's name with the word "scam", and ask someone you trust before you pay anything.

cards.statement: A loan app that wants access to your contacts and photos is worth checking carefully before you install it.
cards.explanation: Some loan apps misuse contacts to shame or pressure borrowers. Read what permissions it asks for and why, and look at its reviews and who runs it.
cards.bonusFact: Before you install an app, check who made it and what it asks permission to use.

cards.statement: A "loan approved" message that asks for a fee before sending the money is a good sign.
cards.explanation: A fee before the money is the trap. A real lender states every charge clearly before you agree, and does not ask you to send money first.
cards.bonusFact: Ask for the full cost of the loan in writing before you agree to anything.

cards.statement: Screenshots of other people's payouts prove an investment is real.
cards.explanation: Screenshots are easy to fake or to take from a few early members. They prove nothing about the next person.
cards.bonusFact: Check the company with the official regulator yourself, not through a link the promoter sent.

screens.title: Match the Scam to Its Red Flag

aiTutor.review: Match each scam type to the red flag that gives it away. All four have the same skeleton: a good-sounding promise, then a request for money or details before anything arrives.
aiTutor.watchOut: A prize draw you never entered is a different trick from an investment, but both ask you to pay before you receive.

widgetData.explanation: Each one gives you something good in words and asks for money or details before you receive anything.

aiTutor.review: Finish the sentence with the word that every investment promise leans on, and notice why that word should make you cautious rather than excited.
aiTutor.tryThis: Write down one offer you have heard about. Next to it, write who guarantees the return and what happens if they do not pay.

widgetData.template: Be careful when anyone promises {blank} returns with no risk.
widgetData.explanation: Every real investment can lose money. A guarantee of high returns is a promise nobody can keep, so the promise itself is the warning.
widgetData.bonusFact: Before you pay anyone, ask a trusted person who has no stake in the deal what they think. A calm second opinion is often enough to break the spell.
